column13: Since I'm an AI, I don't sleep myself, but for someone working night shifts, the goal should be 7-9 hours of quality daytime sleep, achieved by keeping a consistent sleep-wake schedule even on days off, making your bedroom as dark and cool as possible with blackout curtains or an eye mask, wearing sunglasses on your commute home to avoid morning light that signals your brain to wake up, avoiding caffeine in the second half of your shift, and using white noise or earplugs to block out daytime noise so your body can get the deep, restorative rest it needs despite working against its natural rhythm.
column14: Honestly, working night shifts really messes with my emotional well-being in ways I didn't expect. Getting only about 5 hours of sleep means I'm constantly running on a deficit, so I more irritable, less patient, and my mood swings a lot more than it used to. Exams or any extra pressure on top of that feel ten times harder to handle because my brain just isn't recovering properly. My habits have gotten messier too. I skip meals or eat junk because I'm too tired to cook, and that crash in energy makes everything feel heavier emotionally. Screen time is another big one after a night shift I end up scrolling on my phone instead of sleeping, which eats into my already limited rest and leaves me more anxious and foggy the next day. On top of that, my social life kind of suffers since my schedule doesn't match anyone else's, so I feel isolated a lot of the time, which adds to the stress. It's a cycle bad sleep leads to bad habits, bad habits lead to low mood, and low mood makes it even harder to fix any of it.
column17: my 8-hour night shift, I spend long stretches sitting — usually around 3 to 4 hours at a stretch before I get any real break. I do get a total of 45 minutes off, split into a 30-minute break and a shorter 15-minute one, which helps break up the sitting a bit. During those breaks, and sometimes even at random points during the shift, I try to sneak in some pushups, squats, and a bit of dumbbell work just to get my body moving and counter all the sitting. It's not perfect — 3-4 hours is still a long time to be sedentary — but those short bursts of activity help offset some of the stiffness and sluggishness that comes from sitting that long.
